309.title: A song without words
309.hook: Hasidic prayer uses wordless melodies to lift the heart
309.howItsDone: Hasidic communities sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at gatherings called farbrengens or tisches, before prayer and at weddings; many other Jewish communities have adopted them too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebbe of Nemirov chopped wood in secret, and the Litvak said: if not higher. Kindness with no credit.

There's a tune you hum when nobody's listening. In the car. Doing dishes. Rocking a baby at two in the morning. There are no words, or you've forgotten them, and it doesn't matter. The humming settles you. Now picture a long table on a Friday night, a hundred people around it, and the rebbe at the head. Someone starts a slow melody. Yai, dai, dai. Nobody sings a single word. And the whole room starts to rise.
screen: `A TUNE HUMMED IN THE CAR.` → `A HUNDRED PEOPLE AT A TABLE.` → `YAI, DAI, DAI.`

segments.voice: Niggun means melody, and Hasidism made it into something close to a form of prayer. Many niggunim have no words at all, just sounds: yai-dai-dai, bim-bam, ai-ai-ai. Some are slow and aching, some fast and joyful, built for dancing. Every Hasidic community has its own, passed down from rebbe to disciple, some for more than two hundred years. They're sung at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, before prayer, at weddings. Why no words? A saying often attributed to Shneur Zalman of Liadi puts it this way: words are the pen of the heart, but melody is the pen of the soul. Words can only say what you already understand. A melody can carry what you can't put into words: longing, grief, joy, a closeness to God that sentences would only shrink. There's a hint in the Bible, too. When the prophet Elisha needed to prophesy, he said: "But now bring me a minstrel." As the musician played, the hand of the Lord came on him. In Hebrew, the word for playing there comes from the same root as niggun. Music, in that story, opens a door. And a niggun has a shape: it often starts low and slow, repeats and repeats, climbs, then returns. That repetition is the point. By the sixth or seventh time, you stop thinking about the tune. You're just inside it. That's the lift Hasidim are after. Not performance. Not a good voice. Just a heart carried upward on a sound.
screen: `NIGGUN: A MELODY.` · `YAI-DAI-DAI, NO WORDS.` · `THE PEN OF THE SOUL.` · `ELISHA: BRING ME A MINSTREL.` · then, large: `A SONG WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let a simple melody come, any melody, or make one up with three or four notes, and hum it quietly, or inside if you can't make sound. Don't try to sing well; just repeat it, a little slower each time, until you stop thinking about the tune and rest inside it. If you pray, let the melody be your prayer.
Niggun. A Hasidic melody, often with no words, sung over and over until the heart lifts. Words are the pen of the heart; melody, the pen of the soul.
Your line: a song with no words. Where words run out, a melody can still go. Until tomorrow.

310.title: Raising the sparks
310.hook: holy sparks hide in everything, and ordinary acts done with care can lift them
310.howItsDone: Hasidim speak of raising sparks through blessings, prayer and everyday acts done with intention, and in modern usage tikkun olam names acts of justice and repair in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, niggun: a melody with no words, sung over and over until the heart lifts.

You wash a cup. You answer an email. You fold a shirt, buy bread, sweep a floor. Most of your day isn't dramatic. It can feel like the real life, the important, spiritual part, is happening somewhere else, and all this is just maintenance. Hasidism took a picture from the kabbalah that turns that upside down. Hidden inside the cup, the email, the shirt and the bread are sparks of holiness, waiting. And the way you handle them can set them free.
screen: `WASH A CUP. FOLD A SHIRT.` → `JUST MAINTENANCE?` → `SPARKS HIDDEN IN THE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repair, mending, setting something right. The picture behind it comes from Rabbi Isaac Luria, a kabbalist in the town of Safed, whose teachings were written down mostly by his student, Chaim Vital. When God made the world, Luria taught, divine light was poured into vessels that couldn't hold it. The vessels shattered. Sparks of holy light scattered everywhere and fell into the world, trapped in shells, hidden in all things. The work of history is tikkun: gathering those sparks and lifting them back. That sounds cosmic, and it is. But the Baal Shem Tov and the Hasidim brought it down to the kitchen. Sparks wait everywhere, they taught: in food, in work, in conversation, even in the people and places you happen to cross. When you eat with a blessing, work honestly, speak kindly, do an ordinary thing with care, you lift the spark inside it. A related phrase is tikkun olam, repairing the world, and it has old roots. The Mishnah uses it for rules made for the good order of society, and the Aleinu prayer speaks of perfecting the world under the kingdom of the Almighty. In modern times it has become a common name for justice and social action. The Hasidic version is quieter. The repair begins with how you wash this cup, right now.

segments.voice: Choose one small task in front of you, a dish, a bed, a desk, and picture doing it slowly and fully: the water, the fabric, the weight of things. Imagine a spark inside it, waiting for someone to do this well. If you pray, say a word of blessing before you begin.
Tikkun. Repair. In Luria's picture, holy sparks are scattered through everything, and ordinary acts done with care lift them back.
Your line: lift the sparks. The shattered light is waiting in plain things. Day three hundred ten, done.

311.title: The Maggid's circle
311.hook: the Maggid of Mezeritch taught a circle of students who carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe
311.howItsDone: Many Hasidic communities trace their lineage back through their founding rebbe to the Maggid of Mezeritch and the Baal Shem Tov, and they retell the Maggid's teachings at gatherings and on the anniversary of his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun: holy sparks hidden in ordinary things, lifted by doing them with care.

Someone asks a Hasid what Torah he learned from his teacher. His answer, as Hasidim tell it: I didn't go to hear him teach Torah. I went to see how he laces and unlaces his boots. It sounds like a joke. It isn't. Not the lecture, but the way a person lives, down to the laces, can be the lesson. That teacher was the Maggid of Mezeritch, and the students who sat in his house would carry Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
screen: `WHAT TORAH DID YOU LEARN?` → `NOT THE LECTURE.` → `WATCHING HIM LACE HIS BOOTS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Dov Ber was called the Maggid: the preacher, the one who tells. A serious scholar, he came to the Baal Shem Tov, the tradition says, as something of a skeptic, and left as his disciple. After the Baal Shem Tov died, as the tradition tells it, the Maggid became the center of the movement. He wasn't a traveler. He was often ill, and he taught from his home in the small town of Mezeritch, in what is now Ukraine. But the students who came to him were extraordinary. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, who would found Chabad. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, the defense attorney. Zusya of Anipoli, who worried about not being Zusya, and his brother Elimelech of Lizhensk. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, who later led a group of Hasidim to the Land of Israel. And many more. When the Maggid died, something unusual happened. There was no single heir. His students went out across Eastern Europe, and each became a teacher in his own place. One circle in one house turned into many Hasidic communities, each with its own melodies and customs. The opening mishnah of Pirkei Avot includes the charge: raise up many disciples. The Maggid did exactly that. His teaching went out the door, in the boots of his students.

Maggid, meaning preacher, the one who tells. Dov Ber of Mezeritch's students went home after his death and carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
Your line: pass it on. One small house in Mezeritch became many communities. See you tomorrow.

312.title: Opponents and neighbors
312.hook: Hasidism met fierce opposition from the Vilna Gaon's circle; today both ways of life thrive
312.howItsDone: Today Hasidic communities and the Lithuanian-style yeshiva world live side by side in places like Jerusalem, Bnei Brak and Brooklyn, each with its own customs, and study many of the same texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maggid's circle: one teacher in Mezeritch, and students who carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe.

Every family has its big argument. How holidays work. What really matters. Voices get raised, doors get slammed, and for a while it seems there's no way back. Hasidism had one too. It didn't spread without a fight. Some leading rabbis of the time thought it was a dangerous mistake, and said so, loudly. Today: the opponents, and what happened to the argument.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY'S BIG ARGUMENT.` → `HASIDISM DIDN'T SPREAD QUIETLY.` → `THE OPPONENTS.`

segments.voice: Mitnagdim means opponents, the ones who stood against. Their leading figure was Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, called the Vilna Gaon, the genius of Vilna. He and his circle were alarmed by the new movement. The Hasidim changed the prayer book and prayed at their own times. They put enormous weight on the rebbe. Some were accused of neglecting deep Talmud study for joy and song. For communities still shaken by the false messiahs of earlier generations, it looked risky. The community of Vilna declared a ban against the Hasidim. The conflict was bitter: bans on both sides, harsh words, even denunciations to the government. It's not a pretty chapter. The tradition says Shneur Zalman once came to Vilna hoping to make peace, and the Gaon would not see him. But here's the rest of the story. The argument changed both sides. The Gaon's student, Chaim of Volozhin, founded a great yeshiva, and his teaching stressed Torah study as the heart of Jewish life. Hasidism, for its part, held on to both its warmth and its learning. Later, as modern times brought new challenges, the two camps often found themselves on the same side. Today the Hasidic world and the yeshiva world, sometimes called Litvish, from Lithuania, both flourish, often on the same streets. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice that settled an old dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai: these and these are the words of the living God. Two paths. Both endure.
screen: `MITNAGDIM: THE OPPONENTS.` · `THE VILNA GAON.` · `VILNA'S BITTER BAN.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `BOTH PATHS ENDURE.`

segments.voice: Think of a group whose way of doing things rubs you the wrong way: another team, another school, a rival, not an enemy. Ask one honest question: what do they protect that I might forget, what do they get right? You don't have to agree; just find the one true thing in their way, and if you pray, pray for them.
Mitnagdim. The opponents of early Hasidism, led by the Vilna Gaon. The argument was bitter; today both ways of life thrive side by side.
Your line: both paths endure. A bitter argument didn't get the last word. That's day three hundred twelve.

313.title: The story that healed
313.hook: a lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem danced while praying, and began to dance himself
313.howItsDone: Hasidim tell stories of their rebbes at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, and especially on a teacher's yahrzeit, the anniversary of his death, as a way of drawing close to his holiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mitnagdim: a bitter argument with Hasidism that both sides survived. Today, the last of our Hasidic stories.

At a family dinner, someone starts telling a story about a grandparent who's gone, and halfway through, they start doing the voice. The walk. The laugh. For a moment, the person is almost in the room. A good story doesn't just describe something. It brings it back. Hasidim took that seriously. Today, the story they tell about why they tell stories at all.
screen: `DOING GRANDPA'S VOICE.` → `FOR A MOMENT, HE'S IN THE ROOM.` → `A STORY ABOUT STORIES.`

segments.voice: A rabbi, whose grandfather had been a student of the Baal Shem Tov, was once asked to tell a story. He said: a story ought to be told so that it helps. And he told this one. My grandfather was lame. One day people asked him to tell a story about his teacher, the Baal Shem Tov. So he told them how the holy Baal Shem used to leap and dance while he prayed. And as he told it, my grandfather stood up. He got so carried away by the story that he began to leap and dance, to show how his master had done it. And from that hour on, he was healed. That, said the rabbi, is how to tell a story. One small story holds the whole movement inside it. Hasidim didn't treat their tales as entertainment. They told them at the Shabbat table, at the end of a festival, on the anniversary of a teacher's death, believing that telling of a holy deed could stir up the same holiness in the people listening. The story doesn't only remember. It happens again. Look back at this stretch: the Baal Shem Tov and serving with joy, the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, the tailor, the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, the crying baby, the tavern, the rebbe with the axe, the niggun, the sparks, the Maggid's circle, the Mitnagdim. Tomorrow, a new stretch: the Psalms, the songs of Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Pick one story that lifts you, from these Hasidic tales, maybe the shepherd boy's whistle, or from your own life, maybe something your grandmother did. Tell it to yourself quietly, in your own words, the way you'd tell it to a friend, and notice where it lifts. If you pray, give thanks for the people in your stories.
Sippur, Hebrew for a story, a telling. A lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem Tov danced in prayer, and began to dance himself. That's how to tell a story.
Your line: tell it and it happens. A lame man stood up to show the dance. Day three hundred thirteen, and the stretch is done.

314.title: The Psalms
314.hook: one hundred and fifty songs linked to David, woven through every Jewish prayer service
314.howItsDone: Psalms fill the Jewish prayer book, from the morning service to Friday night; many Jews also recite Tehillim privately, in times of trouble, for the sick, and at gravesides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sippur: a lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem danced, and began to dance himself. Today, a new stretch begins.

Walk into a hospital waiting room in Jerusalem and you may see someone rocking gently over a small book, lips moving. On a bus, a teenager doing the same. At a graveside, a whole family. At a wedding, a grandmother. It's very often the same book. Not the prayer book, not the Torah scroll: a collection of one hundred and fifty ancient songs, the one part of the Bible that Jews carry with them almost everywhere. For the next two weeks, let's open it.
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `A BUS, A GRAVESIDE, A WEDDING.` → `THE SAME SMALL BOOK.`

segments.voice: Tehillim is the Hebrew name for the Book of Psalms. It means praises, from the same root as hallelujah. There are one hundred and fifty, gathered into five smaller books. An old midrash notices the pattern: Moses gave Israel five books of Torah, and David gave Israel five books of Psalms. Jewish tradition links the Psalms to King David, the shepherd who played the harp. But the book is honest that it isn't only his. Some psalms are headed for Asaph, some for the sons of Korah, two for Solomon, and Psalm ninety is called a prayer of Moses. Many have no name at all. What's in them? Everything. Praise and thanks, but also fear, anger, loneliness, guilt, homesickness, questions that sound almost like accusations. "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise shall continually be in my mouth." And in the same book: why do You hide Your face? That range is why people reach for them. Whatever you're feeling, a psalm has already felt it. And Jewish prayer is full of them. The morning service opens with a stretch of psalms. Friday night welcomes Shabbat with psalms. Festivals have their own psalms of praise, and each day of the week has its own. Coming up: the tree by the stream, the shepherd, the clean hands, the rivers of Babylon.
screen: `TEHILLIM: PRAISES.` · `150 SONGS IN FIVE BOOKS.` · `DAVID, AND OTHER VOICES.` · `WOVEN THROUGH EVERY SERVICE.` · then, large: `SONGS OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Find a short psalm in a Bible or on your phone: Psalm one hundred seventeen, the shortest in the whole book, is just two verses. Read it out loud, slowly, even in a whisper, then once more, and hear ancient words in your own voice. If you don't have one nearby, sit with the line you heard, at all times, praise; and if you pray, make the psalm your prayer.
Tehillim. The Book of Psalms: one hundred and fifty songs of praise and every other feeling, linked to David and said in every Jewish prayer service.
Your line: songs of praise. One hundred and fifty, with room for every feeling. That's day three hundred fourteen.

315.title: Planted by streams (Psalm 1)
315.hook: the one who delights in Torah is like a tree planted by streams of water
315.howItsDone: Psalm 1 opens the Book of Psalms, so it comes first whenever someone recites Tehillim from the beginning; its tree is often used in Jewish teaching about Torah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tehillim, the Book of Psalms: one hundred and fifty songs of praise and every other feeling. Today, its first page.

Somewhere near where you live there's probably an old tree that has stood through heat waves and storms and whole seasons of your life. What keeps it standing? Not how tall it looks. What you can't see: the roots, and the water they've found. The Book of Psalms could have opened with thunder or kings or battles. Its very first psalm opens with a person, and then a tree.
screen: `AN OLD TREE NEARBY.` → `WHAT KEEPS IT STANDING?` → `THE BOOK OPENS WITH A TREE.`

segments.voice: Psalm one begins with the word ashrei: happy, or fortunate. Happy is the one who doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked, or stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of the scornful. Notice the slide: walking, standing, sitting. It's how people drift: passing by, then lingering, then settling in. Instead, this person's delight is in the Torah of the Lord, and they meditate on it day and night. Then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither." Look at the details. Planted, not wild: someone set it there on purpose, near the water. Streams, plural: channels of water running to it. Fruit in its season: not every day, not on demand, but when the time is right. And the leaf doesn't wither, even in dry weather. Then the contrast. The wicked are like chaff, the husks the wind blows off the threshing floor. Light, rootless, gone. The psalm isn't promising that good people never suffer; the Psalms are too honest for that. It's describing roots. A person who keeps going back to the water, day and night, grows something that holds. And that closes a week: a song without words, raising the sparks, the Maggid's circle, opponents and neighbors, the story that healed, the Psalms, and today, the tree by the stream.
screen: `ASHREI: HAPPY IS THE ONE.` · `WALK, STAND, SIT.` · `A TREE PLANTED BY STREAMS.` · `CHAFF IN THE WIND.` · then, large: `PLANTED BY THE STREAMS.`

segments.voice: Sit where you can see a tree or a plant, or run a little water in a glass and watch it, or just picture one, and think about its roots. Then ask: where are my streams, the text, person, practice or place I keep going back to that keeps me green? Let one come to mind, and if you pray, give thanks for it.
Ashrei, Hebrew for happy, or fortunate, the word that opens Psalm one. Its picture of a person rooted in Torah: a tree by the water, fruit in its season, a leaf that doesn't wither.
Your line: planted by the streams. The leaf doesn't wither. Day three hundred fifteen closes the week.
